name: Theyyam season (North Malabar)
tagline: Mid-November start; ritual performances through the winter and spring
summary: Theyyam season in North Malabar runs roughly November–May, peaking through winter; hundreds of ritual dance-performances take place in village kavus across Kannur and Kasaragod.
description: Theyyam season is the annual ritual period when deities are invoked through elaborate dance, costume and trance in the kavus (sacred groves) and family shrines of North Malabar. It is the living ritual calendar of Kannur and Kasaragod and draws local devotees and curious travellers alike.

The season broadly runs from late autumn into late spring (roughly November–May), with many calendars and local guides noting the season opening in mid-November (Malayalam month Vrischikam) and the densest cluster of performances through winter and early spring.

A visitor sees dozens of different Theyyams — large headdresses, painted faces, fierce masks, and fire rituals — performed on specific, dated festival nights at village shrines. Most events are community rituals rather than staged theatre; Parassinikkadavu (Muthappan) is a noted exception where Muthappan rituals occur on a published daily schedule.
Plan with a local calendar or guesthouse: dates are set by each shrine’s Malayalam-calendar festival, so check an up-to-date Theyyam calendar or district tourism office before you travel.
highlights: Season timeframe: roughly November–May (peak winter months).
Heartland: hundreds of kavus across Kannur and Kasaragod districts.
Daily Muthappan ritual at Parassinikkadavu is an accessible option.
Performances range from midnight-to-dawn ritual nights to daytime offerings.
Each shrine follows its own Malayalam-calendar date; local calendars list hundreds of events.

sections.heading: Background
body: Theyyam is a ritual performance tradition from North Malabar that combines dance, music, costume, and trance to embody local deities and ancestral heroes. Communities maintain specific Theyyams tied to family shrines and village kavus, and performance rights traditionally belong to particular performing communities.

The ritual calendar follows Malayalam months: many references describe the season as beginning in Thulam/Vrischikam and running through Edavam, which maps roughly to the November–May period in the Gregorian calendar.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend a kavu festival night to see full Theyyam: elaborate headgear, face-painting, drums, fire, and communicative trance where the deity is addressed and devotees receive blessings. Popular Theyyams include Muchilottu Bhagavathy, Muthappan, Kathivannur Veeran and regional variants.

Visit Parassinikkadavu Sree Muthappan temple for a reliable option — Muthappan ritual worship there follows a published, frequent schedule and is open to visitors. For village kavus, use a local Theyyam calendar or a trusted guide to confirm dates and directions.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Peak season activity concentrates in winter months (December–March/April) but events run through May; check local Theyyam calendars (district tourism, Theyyam calendar sites, or guesthouses) and confirm before you travel.

Reach remote kavus by road from Kannur or Kasaragod towns; Kannur International Airport (Mattanur) and Kannur and Thalassery railway stations are common gateways. Expect late-night schedules for many kavus and limited signage at shrine sites.

latest.text: Regional Theyyam calendars for the 2026–27 season list the season opening in mid-November (Vrischikam) and show the usual November–May window for Kannur and Kasaragod kavus—confirm specific shrine dates before travel.
TravelKannur and other local calendars note the 2026–27 Theyyam season will begin around November 2026 and publish shrine-by-shrine dates for planning visits.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Mid-November to April (peak winter months December–March).
visitorInfo.howToReach: Use Kannur International Airport (Mattanur) or Kannur/Thalassery railway stations; hire local transport or join a Theyyam tour to reach village kavus—many sites are rural and not well signposted.
etiquette: Confirm shrine dates in advance — each kavu follows its own Malayalam-calendar date; ask your hotel or the district tourism office.
Respect rituals: ask before photographing, avoid flash and intrusive behaviour, and follow shrine-specific rules for entry.
Dress modestly and be prepared for late-night timings, fire rituals and close-up communal activity.
Use local guides or trusted Theyyam calendars to find small, authentic kavus rather than only the tourist sites.
